items.prompt: A force is a push or a ___.

options.why: A colour is not a force. Forces make things move or change shape.
A sound is not a push or a pull.
A smell is not a push or a pull.

hints: Think about how you move a drawer.
There are two kinds of force. One is a push.
What is the opposite of a push?
items.explanation: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can make things move, stop or change shape.

items.prompt: Choose all the things a push or a pull can do.

options.why: Pushes and pulls do not change the colour of things.
A force cannot make something alive.

hints: Think about playing with a ball.
What can your foot or hands make a ball do?
Start with a ball that is still. What can a kick do to it?
items.explanation: A push or a pull can start something moving, stop it or change its direction. It can also change its shape or speed.

items.prompt: Match each action to what the force does.
pairs: kicking a ball that is still
hitting a ball with a bat
hints: Think about what is different before and after each action.
Do the one you are sure of first.
Start with catching. What happens to the ball in your hands?
items.explanation: A kick starts a still ball moving, a catch stops it, a bat changes its direction and pressing clay changes its shape.

items.prompt: Which push will make a ball roll fastest?

options.why: A gentle push makes the ball roll slowly.
A tiny tap makes the ball roll only a little.
Without a push, a still ball stays still.

hints: Think about rolling a ball to a friend far away.
Does a bigger push or a smaller push make it faster?
Compare a tap with a hard push.
items.explanation: A strong push makes the ball roll fastest. A bigger force makes a bigger change in speed.

items.prompt: Bima squeezes the brakes on his bicycle. What happens?

figure.alt: A bicycle with brakes on the handlebars.

options.why: Brakes push against the wheels to slow them.
Turning the handlebars makes a bicycle turn.
Brakes make a force that slows the wheels.

hints: Think about what brakes are for.
Brakes rub against the wheels.
Picture riding down a hill and squeezing the brakes.
items.explanation: The brakes press on the wheels and make a force that slows the bicycle down.

items.prompt: Rina lets a toy car roll down a ramp. Then she makes the ramp higher. What happens?

figure.alt: A toy car at the top of a ramp.

options.why: A higher ramp gives the car more speed, so it goes further.
The car still rolls down the ramp.

options.text: The car rolls back up the ramp.
options.why: Gravity pulls the car down the ramp.

hints: Think about sliding down a tall slide and a short slide.
On which slide do you go faster at the bottom?
Ask: does more speed make the car go further or less far?
items.explanation: A higher ramp makes the car go faster at the bottom, so it rolls further.

items.prompt: How much further did it roll from 3 blocks than 1 block?

figure.caption: Toy car and ramp
head: Ramp height
Distance the car rolled
figure.alt: Table: ramp 1 block high, car rolled 40 cm. 2 blocks high, 75 cm. 3 blocks high, 110 cm.

hints: Find the rows for 1 block and 3 blocks.
Further means the difference between the two distances.
Start with 110 cm and take away 40 cm.
items.explanation: From 3 blocks the car rolled 110 cm. From 1 block it rolled 40 cm. 110 take away 40 is 70, so it rolled 70 cm further.

items.prompt: Is the force a push or a pull? Sort the cards.

items.text: a tow truck moving a car

hints: A push moves something away. A pull moves it closer.
Think about where the force comes from in each card.
Start with the horse. Is the cart behind it or in front of it?
items.explanation: The wind blowing a sailboat, pressing a stapler and squeezing toothpaste are pushes. A magnet lifting a pin, a horse moving a cart and a tow truck moving a car are pulls.

items.prompt: On which surface will a rolling toy car slow down fastest?

options.why: Ice is very smooth. The car slides a long way.
Smooth tiles let the car roll a long way.
Glass is smooth, so the car keeps rolling.

hints: Think about how each surface feels.
Rough surfaces rub against the wheels more.
Ask: which one would be hardest to slide on in socks?
items.explanation: A rough doormat rubs against the wheels the most, so the car slows down fastest. Smooth surfaces let it roll further.

items.prompt: The force that pulls things down towards the Earth is called ___.
hints: It is why a ball falls when you drop it.
It pulls everything towards the ground.
The word starts with g.
items.explanation: Gravity pulls things down towards the Earth. That is why a dropped ball falls to the ground.

items.prompt: Leo drops a big rubber ball and a small rubber ball together. They fall from the same height. What happens?

figure.alt: A big rubber ball and a small rubber ball held at the same height.

options.text: The big ball lands much earlier.
options.why: Many people think this, but balls like these fall together.

options.text: The small ball lands much earlier.
options.why: Being small does not make the ball fall faster.
Gravity pulls both balls down.

options.text: They land at about the same time.

hints: Gravity pulls on both balls.
Neither ball is light and floaty like a feather.
Try it with two balls at home, with an adult.
items.explanation: The two balls land at about the same time. Gravity makes them both speed up in the same way. Only very light things, like feathers, are slowed a lot by the air.

items.prompt: Why does a parachute fall slowly?

figure.alt: A parachute falling slowly through the air.

options.why: Gravity still pulls the parachute down.
A parachute is heavier than air, so it still falls.

options.text: The wind lifts it to the sky.
options.why: It still falls down, only slowly.

hints: The parachute is big and wide.
Think about running with an open umbrella.
Ask: what pushes against the big cloth as it falls?
items.explanation: As the parachute falls, air pushes up against its wide cloth. This slows it down, but gravity still pulls it to the ground.

items.prompt: Sita holds a magnet near a steel paperclip. The paperclip moves before they touch. Why?

figure.alt: A magnet held close to a steel paperclip.

options.why: A paperclip is never alive.
The pull comes from the magnet.

options.text: Sita pushed it with her hand.
options.why: The paperclip moved before anything touched it.

hints: Steel is a magnetic material.
Think about what a magnet does to steel.
Ask: did anything touch the paperclip?
items.explanation: A magnet can pull magnetic things, like steel paperclips, without touching them.

items.prompt: Two magnets push apart when their ends are close. Kofi turns one magnet round. What happens?

figure.alt: Two magnets with their ends close together, pushing apart.

options.why: Turning one round changes which ends face each other.
Turning one magnet round makes different ends meet.
Turning a magnet does not stop it being a magnet.

hints: Each magnet has two different ends.
Turning one magnet changes which ends meet.
Ask: if the same ends push apart, what do different ends do?
items.explanation: Magnets have two ends, called poles. The same poles push apart. When Kofi turns one round, different poles meet and the magnets pull together.

items.prompt: Which one needs the biggest push to get it moving?

options.why: An empty trolley is light, so a smaller push moves it.
A toy car is very light.
A balloon is very light. A tiny push moves it.

hints: Think about how heavy each one is.
Heavier things need a bigger push to start moving.
Picture pushing a trolley before and after shopping.
items.explanation: A full shopping trolley is the heaviest, so it needs the biggest push to start moving.

items.prompt: Draw a child pushing a box and a child pulling a wagon. Use arrows to show each force.

criteria.label: Draws a child pushing a box
Draws a child pulling a wagon
Draws arrows that point the way each force acts

hints: A push arrow points away from the child.
A pull arrow points towards the child.
items.explanation: Arrows show the direction of a force. A push goes away from the child and a pull goes towards the child.
